source: Chen et al. (2023) Teaching LLMs to Self-Debug
finding: Few-shot self-debugging with unit-test feedback and code explanation raises code accuracy. Most of the gain comes from the first debug turn.
numbers: TransCoder C++ to Python (560 problems): Codex 80.4 baseline to 92.5 with unit-test feedback plus explanation. MBPP: Codex 61.4 to 70.8; GPT-4 72.8 to 80.4 (UT).
limits: Unit tests supply the failure signal. Few-shot demos tuned per task. GPT-4 did worse than Codex on Spider.
agent_relevance: Supports G2: the repair step works when it is fed a real failing output.

source: Chen et al. (2023) Teaching LLMs to Self-Debug
finding: Without unit tests (text-to-SQL, Spider), only the model's own explanation is available, and the gain is small.
numbers: Spider dev: Codex 81.3 to 84.1 with explanation; GPT-3.5 71.1 to 72.2; GPT-4 73.2 to 73.6; StarCoder 64.7 to 64.9. Abstract: 2-3 percent, 9 percent on hardest level.
limits: Gain from self-explanation alone is near zero for GPT-4 and StarCoder.
agent_relevance: Without real output the repair signal is weak. Code, not the model, must supply the failure.

source: Chen et al. (2023) Teaching LLMs to Self-Debug
finding: Self-debugging saves samples. One debugged greedy program matches many sampled programs.
numbers: TransCoder: self-debug on greedy beats baseline with 5 samples and is close to baseline with 10 samples (Appendix C.1). Explanation alone, no debugging: +2-3 percent.
limits: Cost counted in samples, not tokens.
agent_relevance: Repair from feedback is cheaper than blind resampling.

source: Huang et al. (2023) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Without external feedback, asking a model to review and fix its own answer makes results worse. Earlier gains came from oracle labels deciding when to stop.
numbers: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 74.7 after 5 calls; CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 41.8. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 89.0; CommonSenseQA 82.0 to 80.0; HotpotQA 49.0 to 43.0.
quote: LLMs struggle to self-correct their responses without external feedback, and at times, their performance even degrades
limits: Reasoning tasks, not code with tests. Prompts for self-correction fixed.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G2: no revision from the model's opinion alone.

source: Huang et al. (2023) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: The mechanism of the drop: the model cannot tell right from wrong, so it flips correct answers to wrong ones more often than the reverse.
numbers: GPT-3.5 GSM8K: 74.7 percent of answers kept after the correction rounds; among changed ones, correct-to-wrong more common than wrong-to-correct. CommonSenseQA: many correct answers changed.
limits: Stated from text and Figure 2; exact flip counts are in the figure.
agent_relevance: A reviewer that cannot detect the defect adds noise. Gate review on a code-found failure (G1, G2).

source: Tyen et al. (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location
finding: Split self-correction in two. Finding the faulty step is where models fail. Fixing it once the step is shown works.
numbers: BIG-Bench Mistake: 2186 chain-of-thought traces, 5 tasks. GPT-4 best at 52.87 overall accuracy for step-level mistake finding; GPT-3.5-Turbo about 10 on word sorting. Humans agree highly.
limits: Traces are PaLM 2 outputs. Simple tasks (word sorting, logic, arithmetic, Dyck, shuffled objects).
agent_relevance: This is the slip-to-defect locating step. Our G2 says code locates; this confirms the model should not.

source: Tyen et al. (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location
finding: Giving the true mistake location and regenerating from there raises accuracy. A random location helps far less.
numbers: Table 6 (accuracy on originally incorrect traces): multistep arithmetic +43.92 with true location vs +20.39 random; Dyck +36.86 vs +21.57; shuffled objects +23.53 vs +11.76. Loss on originally correct traces up to -11 to -15.
limits: Oracle location. They also train a small classifier on out-of-domain data that beats prompting a large model at mistake finding.
agent_relevance: Location information is the bottleneck, so spend code on localization.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation?
finding: When repair cost is counted, self-repair gives modest, uneven gains and sometimes none. The bottleneck is the model's own feedback on its code.
numbers: Replacing the feedback model with a stronger one (GPT-4 feedback for Code Llama, GPT-3.5 feedback, GPT-4 for GPT-3.5 on APPS) beat both baseline and self-repair.
limits: HumanEval and APPS. Compared at equal sample budget.
agent_relevance: Pair a code-run failure with a separate diagnosis step. Do not trust the same model to diagnose its own defect.

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation?
finding: Human debugging feedback beats GPT-4 feedback on the same failing programs.
numbers: 40 failing GPT-4 programs, 2 human explanations each, 16 participants. Repair success: human 62.21 / 45.67 / 14.67 (intro / interview / competition), overall 52.60 percent; GPT-4 feedback 42.64 / 19.33 / 3.67, overall 33.30 percent.
limits: Small human sample (16). Human cost not measured.
agent_relevance: The gap between model and human fault diagnosis is large on hard problems, so a diagnosis scaffold has headroom.

source: Tian et al. (2024) DebugBench
finding: Debugging difficulty depends on defect type. Syntax and reference bugs are easy; logic and multi-bug cases are hard.
numbers: 4,253 instances, C++/Java/Python, 18 bug types. Pass rate gpt-4 / gpt-3.5: missing colons 93.6 / 80.9; operation error 68.6 / 49.5; variable error 63.1 / 52.3; triple bugs 58.9 / 45.5; quadruple bugs 55.9 / 38.7. Human solved 8 to 12 of 12 across types.
limits: Bugs implanted by GPT-4 into LeetCode code, not natural bugs. Zero-shot.
agent_relevance: Defects that span several lines need more than one pass, so plan repeated locate-fix cycles.

source: Tian et al. (2024) DebugBench
finding: Runtime feedback helps for syntax and reference bugs and can hurt for logic bugs.
numbers: Figure 4 (gpt-4-0613): traceback improves syntax and reference error fixing but lowers logic error resolution. Multi-sampling helps logic errors from 1 to 4 samples.
limits: Effect shown mainly in a figure; text states the direction.
agent_relevance: Not every real output is equally good evidence. Low-level tracebacks can mislead on logic faults, so pair output with a test of intent.

source: Zhong et al. (2024) Debug like a Human (LDB)
finding: Segment the program into basic blocks, record intermediate variable values, and ask the model to verify each block. This mimics breakpoints.
numbers: Up to +9.8 percent over baseline on HumanEval, MBPP, TransCoder. HumanEval with GPT-3.5 seeds: 73.8 to 82.9 (LDB) vs 81.1 (Self-Debugging). On Reflexion seeds: 91.5 to 95.1 vs 92.1.
quote: LDB generates the debugging verdicts and explanations based on accurate intermediate values
limits: Needs visible tests and a runnable program. Gains shrink as seed quality rises.
agent_relevance: Concrete in-loop method: per-step state values as evidence at each hypothesis. Fits G2.

source: Zhong et al. (2024) Debug like a Human (LDB)
finding: Self-Debugging with model-written dry-run traces can mislead; real trace values do not.
numbers: Self-Debugging (+Expl., +Trace) failed to improve StarCoder seed programs on HumanEval; LDB did.
limits: Small model (StarCoder). Explanation text is invented, not measured.
agent_relevance: A model's imagined trace is not evidence. Only executed values count.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion
finding: An agent writes tests, runs them, writes a verbal reflection on failures and retries. This reached 91 percent HumanEval pass@1.
numbers: HumanEval Python 91.0 vs GPT-4 80.1. Abstract: +22 percent AlfWorld, +20 percent HotPotQA, +11 percent HumanEval.
limits: Needs generated tests that may be wrong.
agent_relevance: Reflection after a failing run is an existing agent-loop method of the same kind as cognitive-breakdown repair.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion
finding: Ablation on 50 hardest HumanEval Rust problems: no test generation hurts; no self-reflection gives no gain.
numbers: Pass@1: base 0.60; no test generation 0.52; no self-reflection 0.60; full Reflexion 0.68.
limits: One benchmark slice (n=50), GPT-4. Rust compiler gives verbose errors.
agent_relevance: Without a test signal the agent cannot tell whether its code is right, so it makes harmful edits. This supports G1 and G2 together.

source: Jimenez et al. (2024) SWE-bench
finding: Real GitHub issues need localizing a fault across a repo and writing a multi-file patch. Early models fail almost always.
numbers: 2,294 tasks from 12 Python repos. Best model, Claude 2 with BM25 retrieval, resolved 1.96 percent.
limits: Retrieval-only setup, early 2023 models. Later agents score far higher.
agent_relevance: Defines the main real-world testbed where slip-to-defect chains are visible.

source: Yang et al. (2024) SWE-agent
finding: Interface design for the agent matters. Edits with a linting guardrail reduce a common breakdown, repeated erroneous edits.
numbers: Without linting guardrail 15.0 percent (3.0 points lower); no file-editor interface 10.3 percent. 51.7 percent of 2,294 GPT-4 Turbo trajectories had at least one failed edit. Success after any edit 90.5 percent; after one failed edit 57.2 percent.
limits: SWE-agent with GPT-4 Turbo; viewer window of 30 lines or full file also lowered scores (14.3 and 12.7 percent).
agent_relevance: A code check at the edit step stops an introduced slip becoming a defect. Maps to G2 and the code-checked loop.

source: Yang et al. (2024) SWE-agent
finding: Agents succeed fast and fail slow. Failure is mostly wrong implementation, not running out of budget.
numbers: Resolved runs: median cost $1.21 and 12 steps; unresolved: mean $2.52 and 21 steps. 93.0 percent of resolved were submitted before the cost limit. On 248 unresolved SWE-bench Lite trajectories, 52.0 percent were incorrect or over-specific implementation; 23.4 percent cascading failed edits. GPT-4o labeller agreed with authors on 87 percent.
limits: Failure labels assigned by an LLM with 87 percent agreement.
agent_relevance: Long runs signal a stuck loop. A step counter should trigger a change of approach, not more steps.

source: Xia et al. (2024) Agentless
finding: A fixed pipeline (localize, repair, validate) with no model-chosen actions matches or beats complex agents at lower cost. Reproduction tests selected the final patch.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite: 96 fixes (32.00 percent), $0.70. Patch selection ablation: majority vote 77 (25.67); plus regression tests 81 (27.00); plus reproduction tests 96 (32.00).
limits: GPT-4o era. Reproduction tests are model-written and can be wrong.
agent_relevance: Strong support for G2 and G3: code runs checks, model fills slots. The reproduction test checks the failure, not the fix.

source: Xia et al. (2024) Agentless
finding: Benchmark flaws: some issues carry the answer or are unclear. Authors built SWE-bench Lite-S without them.
numbers: 249 problems kept in Lite-S. Problem items include ground-truth patch in the issue and misleading solutions (5.0 percent misleading).
limits: Manual labelling by authors.
agent_relevance: Check what the agent is given before crediting reasoning.

source: Meng et al. (2025) LLM-based Agents for Automated Bug Fixing: How Far Are We?
finding: Six repair systems on SWE-bench Verified are compared on reproduction and localization. Reproduction quality tracks how much reproduction info the issue contains.
numbers: 500 reproduction scripts; 384 (76.8 percent) changed status before and after the golden patch. By issue info: has reproduction code 156 of 194 (80.4 percent); partial 135 of 169 (79.9); natural language only 61 of 87 (70.1); not enough info 32 of 50 (64.0).
limits: Six systems only; Python only. First-author name not checked in text.
agent_relevance: Quality of the failure-reproduction step depends on input evidence. Ask for it or build it before repair.

source: Wang, Pradel, Liu (2026) Are Solved Issues in SWE-bench Really Solved Correctly? (ICSE 2026)
finding: Passing the benchmark tests is not proof of a correct fix. Many plausible patches behave differently from the human patch.
numbers: 7.8 percent of patches counted correct while failing the developer test suite. 29.6 percent of plausible patches differ in behavior; 46.8 percent of those from divergent implementations, 27.3 percent from extra behavior. 28.6 percent of divergent patches certainly wrong. Rates inflated by 6.4 points.
limits: Three tools on SWE-bench Verified (CodeStory, LearnByInteract, OpenHands).
agent_relevance: Core support for G3: a pass on the given tests is not a pass on what the answer was not fitted to.

source: Aleithan et al. (2024) SWE-Bench+
finding: Many SWE-bench successes are leakage or weak tests. Filtering them collapses scores.
numbers: 32.67 percent of passing patches had solution leakage; 31.08 percent suspicious due to weak tests. SWE-Agent+GPT-4 resolution fell from 12.47 to 3.97 percent after filtering and to 0.55 percent on newer issues. Over 94 percent of issues pre-date model cutoffs.
limits: Manual screening of one agent's successes.
agent_relevance: Held-out checks (G3) matter; measured gains may be contamination.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Towards Understanding the Characteristics of Code Generation Errors Made by LLMs
finding: Taxonomy of what model-made defects look like. Errors are often multi-line and structural, not small slips.
numbers: Six LLMs on HumanEval, open coding. Over 40 percent of syntactic characteristics are missing or incorrect code blocks. Most common semantic error: wrong or missing condition. Failures deviate heavily from correct code, so fixes are non-trivial (Finding 3).
limits: Sample of failures coded by two authors (90 percent confidence, 5.5 percent margin). HumanEval only.
agent_relevance: Slip-to-defect maps to requirement misread, wrong condition, wrong block. Repair needs restructuring, not patching.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? (MAST)
finding: A failure taxonomy of agent systems, built from 150 traces and applied to 1600+ traces. 14 modes in 3 groups.
numbers: Inter-annotator kappa 0.88. Failure rate 41 to 86.7 percent across 7 frameworks. Groups: system design 41.8, inter-agent misalignment 36.9, verification 21.3 percent. Reasoning-action mismatch 13.2; no or incomplete verification 8.2; incorrect verification 9.1; premature termination 6.2. LLM judge agreed with humans at 94 percent accuracy.
limits: Mixed tasks (coding, math, agents). Prompt and topology fixes gave +9.4 percent (ChatDev) and +15.6 percent on ProgramDev.
agent_relevance: Many breakdowns are verification failures; a program-held verifier addresses them directly (G3).

source: Chen et al. (2024) REval: Reasoning Runtime Behavior of a Program with LLM
finding: Models are poor at predicting what a program does while it runs, and their answers are inconsistent across related steps.
numbers: Average accuracy 44.4 percent on runtime behavior reasoning; average Incremental Consistency score 10.3; below 20 for all open-source models.
limits: Code LLMs of 2024; prediction without execution. First-author name not checked in text.
agent_relevance: Models cannot simulate runtime state reliably, so supply real traces (as LDB does).

source: Zhang et al. (2024) AutoCodeRover
finding: Program-structure search plus spectrum-based fault localization from tests guides the model to the defect.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite: 19.00 percent at one run ($0.43); 26.00 percent best of 3; ACR-sbfl variant 22.00 percent. Full SWE-bench: 12.42 percent vs SWE-agent 12.47.
limits: Reported numbers from authors; SBFL needs tests that fail.
agent_relevance: Code-side localization is an LLM-agent method already in use (human-style fault localization).
